questions.p:
**Passage I: My Father's Kunafa**

Every Ramadan, my father turns our small kitchen in Mansoura into a kunafa workshop. He is an accountant who spends most of the year __[1] surrounded by numbers, but__ for one month he is happiest with his sleeves rolled up and a copper tray in front of him. When I turned thirteen, he finally decided that I was old enough to help.

Our first job was the dough. My father buys it fresh from a bakery near our building, and the long, thin threads looks like pale, uncooked noodles. He showed me how to pull the threads apart with my fingers and mixing them with melted butter until every strand shone. "Don't hurry this part," he warned. "Dry threads burn. Buttered threads turn golden."

For example, I hurried. After two minutes, I declared the dough ready and reached for the tray. My father lifted a handful of threads and handed them back without a word. I mixed for another ten minutes.

Next came the filling. Some families use cream, but my father insists on a soft white cheese that stretches into long strings when it melts. He pressed half of the dough into the tray, spread the cheese over it, and covered it with the rest. Then he slid the tray into the oven, and we waited.

Waiting was the hardest part. My little brother kept opening the kitchen door to ask whether it was ready. My father, normally a patient man, was totally freaking out and checked the oven every five minutes. At last he took out the tray and poured cold syrup over the hot kunafa, which hissed as the syrup soaked in. My brother and I each grabbed a corner piece, and we burned their tongues because we could not wait.

This year, my father let me make the whole tray on my own. He pretended to read the newspaper, but he looked up every time I opened the oven. I buttered every thread patiently, slowly, and without rushing, and when the syrup hissed over the golden top, he put down his paper and smiled. "Now," he said, "you are ready to teach your brother."
questions.q: Question 1 (underlined portion [1]): Choose the best version of the underlined portion. If the original is best, choose NO CHANGE.
questions.e: Two complete sentences ("He is an accountant…" and "for one month he is happiest…") are joined by "but", so a comma goes before "but" and nowhere else. The strongest wrong choice moves the comma after "but", which leaves the joining word without its comma and puts a comma where no pause belongs.
ce: Correct: a comma before "but" joins two complete sentences.
A semicolon plus "but," is the wrong punctuation: use a comma before "but" only.
The comma belongs before "but", not after it.
A comma cannot split "surrounded by numbers", and the comma before "but" is missing.

**Passage II: The Doctor Who Listened Through Paper**

For centuries, doctors who wanted to hear a patient's heart had only one method: they pressed an ear directly against the patient's chest. This was uncomfortable for doctor and patient alike, and it did not always work. Layers of __[11] clothing, muffled__ the sounds, and in some patients the heartbeat was too faint to hear at all.

In 1816, a young French doctor named René Laennec faced this problem at a hospital in Paris. His patient was a young woman with signs of heart disease, and Laennec felt that pressing his ear to her chest would be improper. In other words, he remembered a game he had seen children play: one child scratched the end of a long wooden beam with a pin, while another child, with an ear pressed to the far end, heard the scratching clearly. Laennec rolled several sheets of paper into a tight tube, placed one end on the woman's chest, and putting his ear to the other. Paris was, at that time, one of the largest cities in Europe. To his delight, the heartbeat sounded louder and clearer than it ever had through his bare ear.

Over the next three years, Laennec tested tubes of different materials and sizes. He finally chose a hollow wooden cylinder that came apart into two pieces. Using it, he listened to the chests of hundreds of patients and recorded the sounds he heard. **Passage III: Big Ears in the Desert**

The fennec fox, the smallest of all foxes, lives in the Sahara and weighs less than many house cats. During the hottest hours of the day, it rests in a cool burrow that it digs in the sand. Its ears, however, are huge for its size, and they do two important jobs.

**Passage V: The Street of the Tentmakers**

Just south of Bab Zuweila, one of the old gates of Cairo, lies a narrow covered street known as the Street of the Tentmakers. Visitors who step in from the busy road outside often stop in surprise at the wall of colour. Its small shops are hung from floor to ceiling with bright panels of __[36] cloth, each__ panel covered in stars, flowers, and curling lines.

The craft is called khayamiya, from the Arabic word for "tent." For centuries, these panels have lined the inside of the large tents that Egyptians put up for weddings and other celebrations. The designs range from simple geometric patterns to detailed pictures of birds and lotus flowers. Each panel is made by hand. A craftsman cuts shapes from scraps of coloured cotton, folds under its edges, and sews them onto a heavy backing with stitches so small and tiny that they are almost invisible.

Today, most celebration tents are covered with cheaper printed fabric. Therefore, the craft has found new buyers: visitors and collectors who hang the panels on their walls as works of art.

**Passage VI: The Bridge That Held**

On the first day of term, our physics __[41] teacher, Mr. Farid wrote__ a challenge on the board: build a bridge out of uncooked spaghetti and glue that could cross a gap of forty centimetres. The team whose bridge held the most weight would win. My partners were Salma, who wanted to become an architect, and Omar, whom had never built anything more complicated than a sandwich.

Salma drew a design full of triangles. She sketched three versions before she was satisfied, each one neater than the last. "Triangles keep their shape under pressure," she explained, "so they make a bridge stronger." Omar and I nodded as if we totally got it.

Building the bridge turned out to be much harder than drawing it. Spaghetti snaps if you hold it the wrong way, and the glue took hours to dry. In contrast, by the end of the first week we had broken two whole packets. Omar, who had seemed so unsure at the start, turned out to have the steadiest hands. He holds each piece in place for a full minute while the glue set. Spaghetti is made from durum wheat, which is also used to make couscous.

On competition day, each team placed its bridge between two desks. Mr. Farid hung a bucket from the middle of each bridge and slowly filled it of sand. One bridge collapsed the moment the empty bucket touched it. Most bridges snapped at two or three kilograms. Ours held five, then six, then seven. As the bucket grew heavier, the room went silent, and nobody said a word.

At nine kilograms, there was a sharp crack, and our bridge folded in the middle. We did not win: a team from the other class had built a bridge that held eleven kilograms. Still, the next morning Mr. Farid pinned a photograph of our bridge on the classroom wall. Omar, who had never built anything before that term, now says he wants to study engineering.
questions.q: Question 41 (underlined portion [41]): Choose the best version of the underlined portion. If the original is best, choose NO CHANGE.
questions.e: Here "Mr. Farid" is extra information that names "our physics teacher", so it needs a matching pair of commas. The original opens with a comma but never closes it. A single comma after "Farid" separates the subject from its verb, and a semicolon cuts off the subject.
ce: Only one comma: the extra information "Mr. Farid" needs a closing comma too.
Correct: a matching pair of commas sets off the name.
A single comma now separates the subject from the verb "wrote".
A semicolon leaves "our physics teacher" alone as a fragment.
